text.title: Product Operations Core Rules
text.summary: 12 testable rules grounding Product Operations plus the universal skip/run routing pair (referenced by the decision tree). The five areas Product Ops owns, the three-level maturity model, AI-native ops patterns, and 2026 adoption stats.

section.title: Background
section.p: Maturity model. Level 1 (Tactical): process documentation, tool management, naming conventions. Level 2 (Strategic): data infrastructure, insights delivery, ceremony design. Level 3 (Transformational): AI automation, predictive analytics, adaptive capacity planning.

AI-native ops patterns. Automated status updates, AI-powered roadmap analysis, predictive capacity planning, and automated stakeholder communication are the four Level 3 patterns. All require Level 1 and Level 2 foundations.
2026 adoption stats. 96% of organizations now have a Product Ops function. 75% of dedicated teams work centralized. 50% report directly to CPO. Top challenge: role clarity and responsibilities.

rule.statement: Product Ops MUST own roadmap tool, experiment platform, feedback ingestion, and metric warehouse plumbing; PMs MUST NOT be on the on-call rota for these systems.
rule.rationale: PMs maintaining their own tooling drift into ops; the explicit handoff is the only structural defence of discovery time.

rule.statement: There MUST be exactly one weekly product-metric rollup (single artefact, single owner, single distribution list); parallel rollups MUST be merged or killed.
rule.rationale: Parallel rollups produce divergent numbers and stakeholder confusion; canonical rollup is the only stable input to QBRs and strategy memos.

rule.statement: Stakeholder updates MUST use the fixed template (north-star metric, weekly delta, top-3 wins, top-3 risks, asks); ad-hoc-shape updates are forbidden.
rule.rationale: Variable-shape updates force stakeholders to re-learn each week and degrade signal-to-noise; the fixed template is the contract.

rule.statement: Every product process (intake, prioritisation, release, postmortem) MUST have exactly one canonical doc in .aidocs/process/; duplicates in Notion/Confluence MUST be marked as mirrors and redirect.
rule.rationale: Process docs in multiple locations diverge; the canonical-location rule plus mirror policy is the only durable single source.

rule.statement: Product Ops MUST attempt to automate a process before requesting headcount; the automation attempt and result MUST be recorded in the request.
rule.rationale: Heading-down-on-headcount-first is the most common cause of Ops bloat; the automation-first rule keeps the function lean.

rule.statement: Pick one canonical store and write all agents against it. Never let agents query Jira and Linear directly for the same question; sync into Postgres or Notion first.
rule.rationale: Cross-system reconciliation is the dominant source of Product Ops debt. A single read surface eliminates the problem permanently rather than managing it query by query.

rule.statement: Define the consumer before building any automation. Every dashboard, digest, and rollup must have a named human reader. If you cannot name one, kill the automation.
rule.rationale: Product Ops debt is mostly orphan reports — automated outputs that nobody reads. Naming the consumer at creation time is the only reliable prevention.

rule.statement: Apply a two-week TTL on every automated insight. Agents stamp every status pack with a freshness window; consumers see "stale" rather than stale numbers presented as current.
rule.rationale: Stale data presented as fresh is worse than no data. An explicit TTL forces consumers to request a refresh rather than act on outdated information.

rule.statement: Agents must enforce maturity progression, not bypass it. Refuse Level 3 requests (predictive analytics, AI roadmap analysis) until Level 1 artifacts exist (template registry, ceremony list, KPI dictionary).
rule.rationale: Skipping Level 1 to Level 3 automates undocumented chaos. The automation codifies the wrong shape and produces confident-sounding wrong answers.

rule.statement: Version templates as code. Roadmap, spec, retro, and OKR templates live in the repo (templates/), not Notion pages. Agents read from the repo so a git diff shows process changes.
rule.rationale: Templates in Notion pages drift untracked. Versioning in git gives an audit trail, enables rollback, and makes template changes visible in code review.

rule.statement: Use PR-style writes for all agent outputs. No agent writes to Jira/Productboard/Notion directly on a fresh observation. Open a draft, post the diff, wait for human acknowledgment, then commit.
rule.rationale: Agent writes that bypass human review create data quality problems that are invisible until a stakeholder meeting. PR-style review catches them at the cheapest point.

rule.statement: Treat Product Ops as three layers: (1) scheduled scrapers pulling state from PM/issue/analytics tools into a normalised store; (2) on-demand subagents for specific asks; (3) a narrow set of write-back automations. Agents propose; humans merge.
rule.rationale: Mixing layers — agents that both ingest and write in the same flow — removes the human review gate that catches agent errors before they reach systems of record.

rule.statement: If preconditions in `## Applies If` do not ALL hold OR any disqualifier in `## Skip If` fires, the agent MUST skip this methodology and document the skip reason in the cycle artefact.
rule.rationale: A minimum-form decision tree must route 'preconditions-not-satisfied' to skip; this rule is the canonical target.

rule.statement: If preconditions in `## Applies If` ALL hold AND no disqualifier fires, the agent MUST run the methodology end-to-end and produce the artefact specified in 02-output-contract.xml.
rule.rationale: Pair to skip-this-methodology; together they form the always-present minimal route.
